newsitem.title: USA: Clinton tax plan a move toward Republicans.
newsitem.headline: Clinton tax plan a move toward Republicans.

text.p: President Clinton's move toward Republicans on items such as capital gains and estate tax relief reduced the likelihood of a veto on tax legislation, some analysts said Tuesday.

Clinton's steps on capital gains and estate tax relief bowed to two key Republican priorities, analysts said. But the president sought more tax relief for college education and to give a $500 child tax credit to more lower-income families.

"If the president can find a way to introduce the proposal he introduced on (June) 30th and veto a bill that's very close to that and make that a winner for him politically, he is a political genius," J.D. Foster, executive director at the Tax Foundation, said.
"What he did by putting his bill in there is he gave himself a more relevant seat at the table, what he gave up was the flexibility of vetoing the final bill," he said.

The House and Senate last week passed their versions of tax cuts and Clinton revealed his new proposal Monday. Final negotiations will start in July in which one bill would be carved largely from the three proposals.

This year the administration got a seat at the table earlier in the process because of an agreement between congressional leaders and Clinton to find a bipartisan solution to wipe out the budget deficit over five years. That pact included $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.
"This Clinton tax bill is interesting in that it's not what you would normally expect from a Democratic bill," said Iris Lav, associate director at the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities.

"It provides as much tax relief to the highest 20 percent as it does to the bottom 60 percent of the income distribution," Lav said. House and Senate bills still give more tax relief to higher-income people, she said.

Clinton proposed allowing 30 percent of profits made on investments such as stocks to be excluded from taxation. The House and Senate bills would cut the top maximum capital gains rate to 20 percent from 28 percent for individuals, which Foster said amounted to a 40 percent exclusion.
Clinton would exclude $2.1 million of family-owned businesses or farms from estate taxes.
Clinton raised the eligibility age for children for the $500 child tax credit to under 17 for the first five years, similar to the House and Senate bills.
But Clinton was criticised by members of his own party for going too far toward the Republicans and not covering enough children in lower-income families with his child tax credit.

"He's given up ground before we sit down," Representative Charles Rangel of New York, the senior Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said in a CNN interview. "People with lower incomes don't receive the full benefit of the tax credit."
Clinton has been careful not to explicitly use the "veto" word ahead of the coming negotiations.
"I think that all parties want a tax bill, the question is what really is acceptable, and I don't think we've seen the bottom lines yet," Lav said.

Analysts generally expect a 20-cent per pack cigarette tax increase in the Senate bill and Clinton's plan to end up in the final product. But key will be reaching agreement on how to use the $15 billion raised from that tax.
"It's the first real tax increase on individuals in the bill," Foster said. The proposed cigarette tax increase would be on top of the current 24-cent-per-pack federal tax.

"What they've done is decided that primarily low-income taxpayers should fund health care for low-income children," he said, adding that 60 percent of the cigarette tax is paid by people with incomes under $30,000.
